newsitem.title: GERMANY: Text of Buba statement on Bonn revaluation plan.
newsitem.headline: Text of Buba statement on Bonn revaluation plan.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Wednesday made the following statement on the German government's plan to revalue central bank reserves. The statement has been translated into English by Reuters.
"The Central Bank Council of the Deutsche Bundesbank at its meeting on May 28 considered the concept of the Federal Finance Ministry to change the accounting procedure of the Deutsche Bundesbank.

The plan involves a significant increase in the value of the gold and currency reserves and the distribution of part of the valuation gain to the Federal Government to redeem debts in the Inherited Debt Redemption Fund. This distribution is to be made already in 1997 and 1998. The plan also involves a reorganisation of capital and reserves.
The Central Bank Council makes the following statement on this:

1. In line with German legislation the Bundesbank has so far adopted valuing reserves at the lowest price principle. The current state of negotiations in the European Monetary Institute indicates that there will be a valuation according to market prices for the European Central Bank and for the consolidated balance sheet of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB), although the non-realised valuation gains will be be put into a revaluation account and not paid out. The ECB Council will make a binding decision on the valuation method in European monetary union.

That also applies to the valuation of the portion of reserves to be transferred by the national central banks to the ECB. The reserves remaining with the Bundesbank will basically remain at the nation's disposal.

2. The concept presented by the Federal Finance Ministry for the years 1997 and 1998 is not in line with rules envisaged for the ESCB because it links the revaluation of reserves with a payout of unrealised income.

3. With entry into European monetary union (EMU) the Bundesbank's tasks will change. The revision of the valuation rules and of the required financial provision should take effect at that time. At the same time the capital structure should be reorganised and the Bundesbank's compensation demands should be replaced. In this context a distribution could be envisaged if it were acceptable in monetary policy terms. It is up to the lawmaker to create the legislation required for this. The Central Bank Council regards it as right that the payout should be used exclusively to reduce the the debt of the Inherited Debt Redemption Fund. The detailed special ruling envisaged so far in the the Federal Finance Ministry's concept for the years 1997 and 1998 can be seen as an intrusion into the autonomous drawing up of the balance sheet and therefore into the Bundesbank's independence. Following the decision on which countries will participate in EMU from the start, the Bundesbank will if necessary take account in its balance sheet for 1997 of a change in the risk situation on the basis of the existing law.
4. A payout in 1997, the reference year for the choice of nations participating in EMU, runs the risk of weakening confidence in the future European currency.

The Federal Government and the Bundesbank have always stressed that the convergence criteria of the Maastricht Treaty must be fulfilled credibly and on a lasting basis in order to put European monetary union on a solid basis.
A formal fulfilment of the fiscal criteria by paying out a valuation gain would in the Bundesbank's view not live up to these requirements.

The payout would only make a limited contribution to the lasting improvement of public finances. In contrast, the negative knock-on effects on the interpretation of the entry criteria and the stability policy credibility of the selection of participants in May 1998 would scarcely be avoidable.
5. A payout of hidden reserves would be controllable in monetary policy terms depending on its size. But if it is legally enforced this would mean an intervention in the Bundesbank's monetary policy.
Such a measure would contradict German tradition and contradict the Maastricht Treaty's view on the independence of the central banks."
